nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the sea ballad, the narrative poem and the Georgian public poem
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and dramatist; the Poet Laureate from 1930 to 1967, the author of 'Sea-Fever' and The Everlasting Mercy, and the most popular English narrative poet of the period.
biography: Born John Edward Masefield at Ledbury, Herefordshire, on 1 June 1878; orphaned young, he went to sea at fifteen, deserted his ship in New York, worked in a Greenwich Village bar and a carpet factory, and returned to England to write. Salt-Water Ballads (1902) and Ballads and Poems (1910) made him famous, and The Everlasting Mercy (1911) caused a scandal by using the word 'bloody' in a narrative poem of country life. He served in the Red Cross in Gallipoli and France, became Poet Laureate in 1930, and died at Abingdon on 12 May 1967.
literary_profile: Masefield revived the English narrative poem and gave the period its most popular sea poetry: 'Sea-Fever' and 'Cargoes' are among the best-known short poems in the language, and The Everlasting Mercy and Dauber brought the country and the sea into the long poem as living speech and story. As Laureate for thirty-seven years he wrote the period's public poetry, and his adventure novels established the historical sea story.
stylistic_characteristics: The rhymed ballad with a strong driving narrative; the sea chantey measure; colloquial and sometimes violent diction in the long narrative poem; the story told by a character in his own voice; the plain, muscular, image-based lyric.
intellectual_concerns: The sea, the ship and the sailor's life; the English countryside and the farming year; the fight, the fair and the boxing booth; the wasted artist (Dauber); England and the public occasion; youth, adventure and the call of the horizon.
historical_significance: Masefield is the period's most popular narrative poet and the Laureate of the Georgian age: 'Sea-Fever', 'Cargoes' and The Everlasting Mercy gave the period its most widely recited verse, his long narratives restored story to English poetry, and his Laureate poems defined the public voice of the period.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the peasant drama, the Aran travel book and the poetic prose of the stage
literary_identity: Dramatist; the greatest dramatist of the Irish revival and the author of The Playboy of the Western World, Riders to the Sea and The Well of the Saints.
biography: Born Edmund John Millington Synge at Rathfarnham, Dublin, on 16 April 1871 into an evangelical landowning family; he read at Trinity College Dublin, studied music and then literature in Germany and Paris, and was sent by Yeats to the Aran Islands in 1898. The Aran Islands (1907) records those visits; In the Shadow of the Glen (1903), Riders to the Sea (1904), The Well of the Saints (1905), The Playboy of the Western World (1907) and Deirdre of the Sorrows (1910) made the Abbey Theatre. He died of Hodgkin's disease in Dublin on 24 March 1909, aged thirty-seven.
literary_profile: Synge is the greatest dramatist of the Irish revival: he made the speech of the Aran and Wicklow people into a poetic prose of extraordinary density, and The Playboy of the Western World is the finest Irish play of the century and one of the great comedies in English. Riders to the Sea is a perfect one-act tragedy, Deirdre of the Sorrows a great verse-prose tragedy, and The Aran Islands one of the finest travel books in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: A poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech; the single cottage set and the one-act compression; the folk tale and the wonder tale as structure; comedy that turns into tragedy without a join; the lyrical final speech.
intellectual_concerns: The Aran Islands and the western seaboard; the sea, drowning and the mother's grief; the peasant imagination and its stories; the wanderer, the tramp and the stranger; the woman, marriage and the arranged match; paganism and the priest; the national character and its myths.
historical_significance: Synge is the greatest dramatist of the Irish revival and one of the finest playwrights in English of the century: The Playboy of the Western World is a permanent comedy, Riders to the Sea a perfect tragedy, and his prose invention — Irish speech made into a literary language — gave modern drama a new music. The Playboy riots of 1907 made him the period's most controversial playwright.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the folk chronicle, the one-act comedy and the institutional making of the Abbey Theatre
literary_identity: Dramatist, folklorist and theatre director; the co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, the collector of Irish folklore and the author of some forty plays.
biography: Born Isabella Augusta Persse at Roxborough, County Galway, on 15 March 1852; she married Sir William Gregory in 1880, was widowed in 1892, and met Yeats in 1896; with him and Edward Martyn she founded the Irish Literary Theatre (1899) and the Abbey Theatre (1904), for which she wrote comedies, tragedies and translations. Her collections — A Book of Saints and Wonders (1906), Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland (1920), Gods and Fighting Men (1904) — preserve the folk tradition, and her journals and memoirs are a central record of the revival. She died at Coole Park on 22 May 1932.
literary_profile: Lady Gregory is the practical founder of the Irish national theatre and the preserve of its folklore: without her money, her management and her plays there would have been no Abbey Theatre. Her one-act comedies (Spreading the News, The Rising of the Moon, The Workhouse Ward) are the finest of their kind in English, Gods and Fighting Men is the great popular compendium of Irish myth, and her translations of the Cuchulain cycle gave Yeats his material.
stylistic_characteristics: The one-act comedy with a comic misunderstanding and a mock-heroic close; the Anglo-Irish dialect written phonetically; the folk tale transcribed and shaped for the stage; the plain prose of the collector who records rather than embellishes.
intellectual_concerns: Ireland and the Irish peasantry; the folklore, the fairies and the saints; the landlord and the tenant; the police, the prison and the law; the workhouse and the emigrant ship; the national past and the Cuchulain cycle.
historical_significance: Lady Gregory is the co-founder and practical manager of the Abbey Theatre and the period's great collector of Irish folklore: she wrote some forty plays, preserved the myths in Gods and Fighting Men, and her journals are the indispensable record of the revival. Without her there would be no Irish national theatre.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Dublin tenement tragedy and the politicised tragi-comedy
literary_identity: Dramatist and autobiographer; the great working-class playwright of Dublin, the author of the Abbey Theatre's three great tenement plays, and the finest Irish memoirist of the century.
biography: Born John Casey in a Dublin tenement on 30 March 1880 into a poor Protestant family; he worked as a labourer, a railwayman and a docker, joined the Gaelic League and the Irish Citizen Army, and took part in the 1916 Rising's periphery. The Shadow of a Gunman (1923), Juno and the Paycock (1924) and The Plough and the Stars (1926) made him the Abbey's greatest discovery; the riot that greeted The Plough drove him to England in 1926, where he wrote The Silver Tassie (1929), Within the Gates (1934), Red Roses for Me (1942) and the six-volume autobiography. He died at Torquay on 18 September 1964.
literary_profile: O'Casey wrote the greatest working-class tragedy in English: Juno and the Paycock and The Plough and the Stars made the Dublin tenement and the Easter Rising the subjects of a tragic art, and his tragi-comic idiom — the rhetoric of 'the patter of the blows' — is one of the period's great inventions. The Silver Tassie, with its expressionist second act, opened the Irish theatre to European experiment, and his autobiography is the finest Irish prose of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The tragi-comedy that turns from farce to tragedy in a single scene; the tenement speech of Dublin rendered phonetically; the choric commentators (Juno, Bessie Burgess); the expressionist act inserted into a realistic play; the ballad and the song as structural device.
intellectual_concerns: The Dublin tenement and the Dublin poor; the Easter Rising and the war of independence; poverty, drink and the pawnshop; the mother's grief and the son's death; the Church, the Union and the Citizen Army; the emigrant and the emptied city.
historical_significance: O'Casey is the greatest working-class dramatist in English and the central Irish playwright after Synge: the three Abbey plays are permanent, The Silver Tassie brought expressionism to the Irish stage, and his autobiography is the period's finest Irish prose. The riots against his plays are the period's clearest evidence of the writer's collision with nationalism.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the modernist novel, the short-story sequence and the language of the night
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and poet; the greatest prose innovator of the century and the author of Ulysses and Finnegans Wake.
biography: Born James Augustine Aloysius Joyce in Rathgar, Dublin, on 2 February 1882, the eldest of ten children of a rate collector who ruined the family; he was educated by the Jesuits at Clongowes and Belvedere and at University College Dublin, left for Paris in 1902, returned for his mother's death in 1904, and left Ireland for good with Nora Barnacle in October 1904. He taught in Pola and Trieste, published Chamber Music (1907), Dubliners (1914), A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) and Ulysses (1922), moved to Paris in 1920, and published Finnegans Wake in 1939. He died in Zurich on 13 January 1941.
literary_profile: Joyce is the greatest prose writer of the century: Dubliners invented the modern short-story sequence, A Portrait of the Artist invented the novel of the aesthetic consciousness, Ulysses made the single day and the single city the frame for every style at once, and Finnegans Wake dissolved the English language into a dream. He is the central figure of modernist fiction, the model for the experimental novel, and the writer who made Dublin the most completely rendered city in literature.
stylistic_characteristics: The epiphany and the open ending (Dubliners); free indirect style perfected in the Portrait; the interior monologue and the parody of every style (Ulysses); the portmanteau word and the dream-syntax (Finnegans Wake); the exact topography of a real city; the musical phrase and the recurring motif.
intellectual_concerns: Dublin and the paralysis of the Irish city; the artist and the making of a soul; the family, the father and the mother; sex, the body and the Church; exile and the remembered homeland; language itself and the whole history of style; death, resurrection and the ordinary day.
historical_significance: Joyce is the greatest novelist of the period and the central figure of modernism: Dubliners made the modern short story, A Portrait of the Artist created the novel of the artist, Ulysses is the most influential novel of the century, and Finnegans Wake is the most radical work of prose in English. He is the writer against whom all subsequent experimental fiction measures itself.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the modern biography, the debunking essay and the Bloomsbury polemic
literary_identity: Biographer and critic; the author of Eminent Victorians, the founder of modern literary biography and the most brilliant English prose satirist of the period.
biography: Born Giles Lytton Strachey in London on 1 March 1880 into an Anglo-Indian military family; he read at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he joined the Apostles, and lived in Bloomsbury from 1905. Landmarks in French Literature (1912) preceded Eminent Victorians (1918), which made him famous and transformed biography; Queen Victoria (1921) won the James Tait Black Prize, and Elizabeth and Essex (1928) was his last great work. He died at Ham Spray, Wiltshire, on 21 January 1932.
literary_profile: Strachey invented modern biography: Eminent Victorians took four Victorian sages — Manning, Florence Nightingale, Arnold and Gordon — and reduced them with irony, psychology and a novelist's sense of scene, and every literary biographer since has worked in its shadow. Queen Victoria is the most admired short life in English, and his prose — epigrammatic, witty, perfectly controlled — is the period's finest satirical style.
stylistic_characteristics: The short, ironic, epigrammatic life; the revealing detail chosen for its absurdity; the sudden shift of tone from solemnity to bathos; the long periodic sentence with a sting in the tail; the narrative scene in which the subject is caught unawares.
intellectual_concerns: The Victorian age and its sages; the discrepancy between public reputation and private life; power, ambition and the will; religion and its functionaries; the biography as an art form and a moral instrument; the English ruling class and its illusions.
historical_significance: Strachey founded modern English biography: Eminent Victorians changed how lives are written, Queen Victoria remains the finest short life in English, and his prose gave the period its most brilliant irony. Every twentieth-century biographer who debunks or humanises a subject works in his debt.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Landmarks in French Literature (1912); Eminent Victorians (1918, biography); Queen Victoria (1921, biography); Books and Characters (1922, essays); Florence Nightingale (1922); Pope (1925, lecture); Elizabeth and Essex: A Tragic History (1928); Portraits in Miniature (1931, essays); Characters and Commentaries (1933, posthumous); The Letters of Lytton Strachey (2005, posthumous); Spectatorial Essays (1964, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the art criticism of the Post-Impressionists and the formalist essay
literary_identity: Painter, critic and curator; the man who brought Post-Impressionism to England, the founder of the Omega Workshops, and one of the period's most influential art writers.
biography: Born Roger Eliot Fry in London on 14 December 1866 into a Quaker family; he studied natural sciences at Cambridge and painting in Paris and Italy, worked as a critic for the Athenaeum and the Burlington Magazine, and organised the two Post-Impressionist exhibitions in London (1910 and 1912) that changed English painting. He founded the Omega Workshops in 1913, became Slade Professor at Cambridge in 1933, and died in London on 9 September 1934; Virginia Woolf's biography of him appeared in 1940.
literary_profile: Fry is the great English art critic of the period: the 1910 exhibition introduced Cézanne, Gauguin, Van Gogh and Matisse to England, and his formalist criticism — Vision and Design (1920), Transformations (1926), Cézanne (1927) — gave English writing about art a new vocabulary and a new seriousness. The Omega Workshops made modern design a Bloomsbury enterprise.
stylistic_characteristics: The formalist description of a picture — line, mass, colour and the organisation of the surface; the conversational lecture; the polemical review; the plain, exact, unmystical prose of the working painter.
intellectual_concerns: The formal qualities of art and the independence of the aesthetic; Post-Impressionism and the modern movement; the decorative and the applied arts; Italian painting and the classical tradition; criticism as a profession.
historical_significance: Fry made modern art visible in England: the Post-Impressionist exhibitions of 1910 and 1912 introduced the century's painting to a British public, his criticism established formalism as a method, and the Omega Workshops made modern design practical. He is the period's central art writer.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Giovanni Bellini (1899); A Catalogue of the Paintings at the Johnson Collection (1913); Vision and Design (1920, essays); Transformations (1926, essays); Cézanne: A Study of His Development (1927); Flemish Art (1927); Characteristics of French Art (1932); Henri-Matisse (1930); Last Lectures (1939, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the first English stream-of-consciousness novel and the woman's life in sequence
literary_identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of Pilgrimage, the first sustained English novel of consciousness and the finest fictional record of the independent woman writer of the period.
biography: Born Dorothy Miller Richardson in Abingdon on 17 May 1873; her family's finances collapsed with her father's bankruptcy, and she left school at seventeen to teach, working in a Hanover school and in a London office. Pointed Roofs (1915) began Pilgrimage, a sequence of thirteen novels that she published over twenty years and never completed; she was associated with the Freewomen and with the modernist little magazines, married the artist Alan Odle in 1917, and died at Beckenham on 17 June 1957.
literary_profile: Richardson is the inventor of the English stream-of-consciousness novel: Pointed Roofs preceded Ulysses by seven years and gave the technique its first sustained English use, and Pilgrimage is the fullest fictional record of a woman's consciousness making itself in the period. Her sequence is the great alternative to Joyce and Woolf, and her essays on the woman novelist are among the period's sharpest feminist criticism.
stylistic_characteristics: The interior monologue uninterrupted by an explaining narrator; the present tense of perception; the sentence that records rather than describes; the refusal of plot in favour of the texture of experience; the recurring image that surfaces across volumes.
intellectual_concerns: The woman's consciousness and the woman's work; the school, the office and the lodging house; poverty and the class of the shabby-genteel; friendship between women; the artist's formation; London and the rented room.
historical_significance: Richardson wrote the first English stream-of-consciousness novel and the longest fictional record of a woman's inner life in the period: Pointed Roofs opened the way for Joyce and Woolf, Pilgrimage is a central modernist sequence, and her work is the foundation of the English novel of female consciousness.
